o1.biggest_strength: Every rule comes from our own numbers. Break-even is $27.10 on the first order and $38.46 over 90 days, and the kill, learning and stop lines all derive from them. The budget sums exactly to $30,000. Hooks use Maria's and Tasha's actual words.
o1.biggest_mistake: It is very dense with tables, so it reads like a spreadsheet for some of the team. The day-20 release rule also lets TikTok-reported cost count as one of its three votes.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a short plain-language summary of who does what on Monday. Drop the platform-reported read from the release rule, or make it secondary to the store tags and survey.

o2.biggest_strength: It is clean and easy to hand off. Set-up is thorough (dedupe, domain verification, comment moderation), the budget sums correctly with a reserve, and named owners are listed. It also plans to own rights before the March licences end.
o2.biggest_mistake: The hooks lean less on our customers' own lines and leave out 'My feet don't ache by hour ten'. The day-30 order-count target of 790 assumes the full $30k is spent, even though $1k is a conditional reserve. The $76 no-purchase kill is aggressive for a new pixel.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Write hooks directly from Maria's and Tasha's quotes. Align the day-30 order bar with actual spend. Add a geo holdout for a cleaner incrementality read.

reason: Both are usable and correct, but the first ties every threshold to our margins and uses our customers' words. Its holdout idea gives a cleaner read on whether TikTok actually adds customers. The second is easier to read and better for team hand-off, but slightly less sharp.
